Part 10 Multi-Circle Objects and Joint States ​

Analyzing a single object or circle[1] often compresses other conditions into a black box called “environment.” Multi-circle analysis brings into one joint state the structural units that can change the path of an event and that can be distinguished by boundaries, relations, channels, and time windows. The aim does not require adding background without limit. Families, teams, institutions, platforms, markets, cultural communities, bodily systems, and geographic spaces can all matter in the same event. Naming them does not automatically supply grounds for object facts about them or support for a grouping gain (§4.3).

10Note

Understanding this section

Part X: Multi-Circle Objects and Joint States

This part decomposes “the environment affected them” into distinguishable objects, relations, and channels. Decomposition is justified when these differences change the path in question; listing many background factors is not a reason to put all of them into a model.

Chinese source line 2180 calls conditions easily omitted by a single-focus model the “environment” black box. The criticism concerns hiding structural differences that actually affect the answer, not prohibiting environmental variables. Sometimes one measured background quantity suffices for a narrow question; further decomposition into objects is justified only when its internal roles, transmission, and constraints need tracing. [T-intro; T-simple]

A joint state describes several distinguishable units together while preserving their boundaries and local states. Not all objects must be of one type: bodily systems, families, institutions, platforms, and geographic spaces may participate in one event through different relations. Their being “simultaneously important” still requires support from the task and material; an author's list of names does not complete object admission. [T-intro; T-joint]

To decide whether a unit deserves distinction, first ask whether changing it or its channel would change possible event paths or the difference to be explained; then ask whether material supports its boundary, relation, and time window. The first question generates candidate importance, while the second constrains explanatory strength. An attractive counterfactual story is only a research lead, not a substitute for actual comparison or a way to turn every imagined factor into an established cause. [T-intro; T-101]

Boundaries specify who and what is included; relations specify connections; channels specify what can travel where; time windows specify when these arrangements hold. Together they prevent “family, markets, and culture all affect them” from becoming an uncheckable total explanation. Family members need not all receive identical information, platform exposure is not unified opinion, and the same institution may change rules between periods. [T-intro; T-D0]

This part continues Part IX's actor states rather than erasing the individual. It next establishes candidate circles and the definition of the joint object, distinguishes relations, multiple memberships, material and meaning, and asynchronous clocks, then fixes joint snapshots, perturbs boundaries, and checks complexity. Specific future transmission still requires event-driven analysis; a structural diagram alone cannot prove that a future path must occur. [T-intro; T-stop]

This introduction states an analytical task and scope; it does not report an experiment in which a multi-circle model has already won. The following §10.1 uses actual expenditure-tracking literature to show how boundaries and interfaces obtain material. Here a wholly artificial two-segment channel explains why “resources exist upstream” may not answer how much reaches the endpoint. The examples retain separate statuses and proof responsibilities. [T-intro]

Multi-circle analysis must separately record object facts and grouping gain for the task. Actual family members, institutional relations, and excluded positions need not first improve prediction to be acknowledged. Corresponding comparison responsibilities arise only when claiming that another grouping layer improves explanation or foresight. Simplification also cannot delete independent rights or responsibility facts because gain is insufficient.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Clarify the original question and differences currently omitted by the simple representation; adding objects is not the default objective.

  2. 2

    Decompose background factors that may alter paths into candidate units, specifying boundaries, relations, channels, and windows.

  3. 3

    Obtain corresponding material for each unit; shared naming confers neither object status nor unified subjecthood.

  4. 4

    Preserve actors and local differences, checking whether a simple representation already suffices.

  5. 5

    A static joint representation supplies only a starting point for later transmission analysis, not premature conclusions about the future, values, or permissions.

Distinctions to keep clear

Environmental variable

A background quantity sufficient for a narrow task.

≠

Environmental black box

One word conceals important transmission and differences.

Joint representation

Preserves multiple units and cross-boundary relations in parallel.

≠

One enormous unified subject

Joint inclusion in a model cannot generate shared consciousness or will.

Candidate importance

A research reason that a condition may change the answer.

≠

Established effect

Requires corresponding material and comparisons.

Mathematical teaching construction: identical upstream stock, different attainable endpoint quantitiesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA wholly artificial single-period channel model. Sending at the limit is an explicit premise; otherwise min supplies only an upper bound.

Suppose upstream holds 10 units of teaching resources, endpoint demand is at least 10, and the first and second channel segments have delivery limits q1 and q2. With no loss or other sources, and actual sending at the feasible limit, endpoint receipt in the current period is min(10,q1,q2). Scenario A, (q1,q2)=(10,10), receives 10; scenario B, (10,2), receives 2. Stock 10 alone cannot distinguish outcomes, but recording the second interface can. If the task asks only upstream stock, the two transmission segments need not be expanded for that question.

BoundaryThese are not national-budget or organizational-behavior data and do not establish grouping-gain support for any multi-circle grouping.

10.1Treating a Circle as a Candidate Object ​

In briefA circle's candidate definition is a contestable specification of an object: whom it includes, on what grounds, how positions and channels differ, and when it still counts as the same object. It first makes the question discussable; improved prediction is a separate claim requiring comparison.

As a candidate object, a circle can be represented as follows.

C* = <所指的圈层，候选边界，成员资格，角色规则，进入与退出，内部状态，外部接口，物质通道，体验—意义通道，约束，时间窗，尺度剖面，同一性判据，证据状态，反例>.[2]

“Several similar people” does not suffice to define a circle. A circle need not have shared consciousness or a unified goal. Members may not know that the analyst has grouped them into the same circle. They may disagree about goals, and a candidate structure may form solely through shared exposure to the same platform, rule, space, or risk. Documents, memberships, sustained interactions, or shared exposure can support the corresponding facts about the object. A further claim that adopting this grouping improves explanation or foresight requires testing for a gain within the stated scope against a complexity-matched alternative grouping or no-grouping baseline. Support from a grouping-gain test concerns eligibility for this latter, task-specific claim. It does not decide whether the organization, relationships, or people affected exist.

Admission QuestionEvidence RequiredIf the Check Does Not Pass
Can the boundary be distinguished?Membership rules, interfaces, shared exposure, or sustained interactionRetain it as the analyst’s grouping and do not call it an objective circle
Is there differentiated structure within it?Roles, relations, channels, or constraintsReclassify it as a population category or an environmental variable
If a grouping gain is claimed, does the grouping improve explanation or foresight?Out-of-sample comparison with a simple baselineDo not claim that a gain has been established. Retain facts about the object that have independent grounds. Depending on the task, fall back to a single focus, continuous variables, or a candidate grouping
Does identity hold within the time window?The identity criterion, entry and exit, and conditions for conversion and dissolutionRecord separate segments, or record an object conversion
Have counterexamples been retained?Boundary perturbation or review across time or locationsReport the sensitivity and narrow the related conclusions; a grouping gain already claimed is handled under §4.3
10.1Note

Understanding this section

10.1 Treating a Circle as a Candidate Object

A circle's candidate definition is a contestable specification of an object: whom it includes, on what grounds, how positions and channels differ, and when it still counts as the same object. It first makes the question discussable; improved prediction is a separate claim requiring comparison.

C* at Chinese source line 2186 contains fifteen items. It is not synonymous with an everyday ‘circle of friends,’ nor must its members be united, similar, or acquainted. Line 2188 explicitly says a circle ‘need not have shared consciousness or a unified goal’. People sharing rules, platforms, spaces, or risks may form a candidate structure even without knowing one another, but ‘candidate’ cannot be omitted. [T-101]

The first group comprises the circle referred to, the candidate boundary, and membership. The circle referred to provides stable reference, not evidence; the boundary specifies included people, states, relations, or exposure; membership specifies the grounds for deciding inclusion. An analyst including someone within a shared-risk scope does not mean that person voluntarily joined an organization, knows the classification, or consents to data sharing. Boundaries and membership should permit unknowns, disputes, and exceptions, not force binary classification just to draw a circle. [T-101；T-members]

The second group comprises role rules and entry/exit. Roles specify information, tasks, or costs associated with different positions; entry/exit states start and end, grounds, conditions, and actual feasibility. Nominal members may be inactive, while informal participants may bear risks. Analytical exit, termination of formal status, and actual cessation of exposure need not coincide. [T-101；T-members]

The third group comprises internal states and external interfaces. Internal states record grounded quantities relevant to this task, potentially requiring distributions or positional differences; external interfaces record points of input, output, filtering, and transformation. A circle mean alone does not reveal every member, and simultaneous environmental changes do not establish direct interfaces between circles. [T-101；T-joint]

The fourth group comprises material channels, experiential–meaning channels, and constraints. How funds, time, equipment, care, or action conditions flow differs from how notices are understood or trust forms or is damaged. The two may interact, but each requires specified carriers. Constraints limit possible transmission or action. A common slogan alone does not establish shared experience, nor does resource allocation establish actual usability at endpoints. [T-101；T-channels]

The fifth group comprises time window, scale profile, and identity criterion. The window limits this observation and the validity period of relations. The scale profile states aggregation, space, time, organization, causality, observational resolution, influence, network topology, and jurisdiction/authorization axis by axis. Retain a reasoned “not applicable” for genuinely inapplicable axes and “unknown” for insufficient evidence; do not delete axes. The identity criterion specifies how much membership turnover, institutional change, or platform migration still permits reference to the same object, and when segmentation or recording an object conversion becomes necessary. [T-101；T-SP；T-D0]

The final two items are evidence status and counterexamples. Evidence status distinguishes documents, participation records, interaction, common exposure, and inference, including unknowns and conflicts. Counterexamples require more than an extra ‘exceptions are possible’: specify which boundary changes, time transfers, or evidence elsewhere would change support. Listing a counterexample does not establish passage of a falsification test; unperformed reviews remain unchecked. [T-101]

The table first asks whether the boundary can be distinguished, using membership rules, interfaces, common exposure, sustained interaction, or similar evidence. If the current boundary has only an analyst's name without corresponding grounds, retain it as an analyst grouping rather than calling it an objective circle. This does not deny people's existence; it limits the claim that ‘these people actually form the stated structure.’ [T-101]

The second question asks whether there is differentiated internal structure, requiring roles, relations, channels, or constraints. Selecting similar people by age or preference may define a demographic category without constituting a circle for this task. Conversely, if age rules actually determine admission, obligations, or exposure, examine those structures rather than declaring age categories always structureless. If no corresponding structure is found, use a demographic category or environmental variable; every statistical slice need not be called a circle. [T-101]

The third question begins conditionally: ‘If a grouping gain is claimed’. Existing documents and interactions may support the existence of organizations, relations, or affected people. Whether a specific grouping improves explanation or foresight over alternative representations requires a separate complexity-matched out-of-sample comparison. Support from a grouping-gain test (§4.3) is precisely this latter kind of task-relative eligibility, neither an adjudication of ultimate ontology nor a decision about recognizing affected people based on prediction scores. [T-101；T-D0；T-G1]

Even the minimum positive grouping-gain claim requires more than a table of lower errors: predefine the object, grouping, scale, time window, identity criterion, target, metric, threshold, and data split; address common environments, sampling/classification biases, and leakage; compare with a complexity-matched null model that does not use that grouping information; then check boundary perturbations and independent time blocks or sites. On failure, claim no gain and return as appropriate to a single focus, continuous variables, or candidate grouping, retaining independently grounded object facts. Failure of the positive criterion does not automatically establish the null model; null conclusions have their own test criteria. [T-G1；T-contract]

The fourth question is identity within the window, requiring the identity criterion and conditions for entry, exit, transformation, and disintegration. For example, a short-term collaboration group may still satisfy the specified identity criterion after renaming, or may become a new object through changed membership, rules, or interfaces; an unchanged name does not guarantee that the identity criterion holds either. When conditions fail, segment records or record an object conversion instead of silently pooling new and old material as one stable sample. [T-101；T-change]

The fifth question is whether counterexamples are retained and seriously addressed. Changed membership thresholds or another period or site may weaken or reverse conclusions. Downgrade affected claims rather than redrawing boundaries to retain only favorable outcomes. Specify the grounds and scope of boundary perturbations beforehand; arbitrary redefinition is not review of the original claim. [T-101；T-change；T-G1]

The Uganda grant-tracking study's value here lies in distinguishing central, district, and school records and transmission stages; it did not first establish that a circle model predicts better before recognizing schools' existence. The study itself made no pre-registration of a grouping-gain test under this book's current requirements. It therefore supports only the stated historical interfaces and receipt facts under its original design, without conferring formal grouping-gain eligibility here. [P-UG；T-101]

Ultimately retain two different answers: how far evidence supports the object, and how far it supports the benefit of this grouping for the task. The former may have reliable sources while the latter remains unevaluated; a statistical grouping may also aid a task without licensing invention of a unified acting subject. Separating them prevents invalid leaps between model performance and people's existence, willingness, or rights. [T-101；T-G1]

A circle's candidate definition is not a license to exist. First list object grounds such as documents, interaction, exposure, and relations, then carry out a grouping-gain test only when grouping gain is actually claimed. If a single focus or continuous variables suffice for the current prediction question, use that simpler representation while separately retaining real members, affected people, and responsibility relations.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Declare all fifteen items, distinguishing naming, object evidence, and task gain; a complete definition does not establish a valid object or model.

  2. 2

    First check boundaries and differentiated internal structure; if insufficient, retain candidate grouping or return to demographic categories/environmental variables.

  3. 3

    Use the identity criterion and the window to test whether identity continues; otherwise segment records or record an object conversion.

  4. 4

    Enter the corresponding grouping-gain test only when claiming grouping gain, setting down the test conditions beforehand and addressing bias, leakage, and complexity.

  5. 5

    Compare predefined out-of-sample results and check boundary perturbations and independent times/sites; a single training fit cannot substitute.

  6. 6

    Record support, failure, or unknowns claim by claim; no positive support does not automatically support the null model or erase independent object facts.

  7. 7

    Retain counterexamples, sensitivity, and bounded uses; grouping does not confer unified consciousness, value, responsibility, or authorization.

Distinctions to keep clear

Circle referred to

A name pointing to a candidate object.

≠

Support for object facts and grouping gain

Requires actual evidence of boundaries, members, relations, or exposure.

Similar demographic category

Classification by a characteristic may have statistical uses.

≠

Differentiated structure of a circle

Requires roles, relations, channels, or constraints relevant to this task.

Facts about an existing object

May be independently supported by documents, activities, or observations.

≠

Grouping gain

A conditional task advantage over complexity-matched alternative representations.

Common exposure

Shared risks, rules, or platform conditions.

≠

Shared consciousness and voluntary commitment

Do not automatically follow from inclusion within the same scope.

Grouping gain not supported

May reflect failure or insufficient comparative evidence.

≠

Null model supported

Requires an independent predefined null-conclusion criterion.

Continuation under the same name

The reference label has not changed.

≠

Identity holds

The identity criterion must have actual support within the window.

Teaching construction: shared exposure to a water outage is not shared willTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAn entirely fictional scenario; the branch, period, and evidence availability are teaching assumptions, not an actual water outage.

Suppose a specified water-supply branch is shut off Monday from 8 to 12, with legitimately obtainable equipment diagrams and field records identifying its interfaces. That scope may be recorded as a candidate common-exposure structure, distinguishing endpoint locations, stored-water conditions, and other supplies. Residents being strangers with different goals does not cancel supported common exposure. However, pipe-network boundaries cannot establish identical actual water shortages, shared support for a protest, or authorization of a representative to speak.

BoundaryCommon exposure provides entry to object evidence; it does not automatically establish predictive advantage for a specific grouping or a unified agent.

Mathematical teaching construction: even equal-complexity groupings can fail across timeTeaching scenario

AssumptionsGroupings, values, and training/test order are entirely constructed. The alternative does not use g's information, both have two estimable means, and neither is re-estimated during testing.

Take four constructed units, candidate grouping g={1,2}/{3,4}, and alternative grouping n={1,3}/{2,4}. Each model uses two group-mean parameters, estimated once only in the training block. Training targets are (0,0,2,2); g predicts (0,0,2,2), while n predicts (1,1,1,1), giving MSE 0 and 1 respectively. After setting down predictions, targets in another artificial time block become (2,2,0,0). Each of g's squared errors is 4, so MSE=4; each of n's is 1, so MSE=1. Thus g's training advantage of 1 over n becomes a loss disadvantage of 3 in this test block.

BoundaryA logical counterexample only, not a real grouping-gain test or proof that all groupings fail. There is no pre-registration, independent repetition, or power requirement for a null conclusion here; the numerical example is not empirical validation of this book.

Teaching construction: reliable object facts can coexist with unevaluated gainTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe association and materials are teaching assumptions; material reliability and scope of support are explicit premises.

Suppose an association's registration documents, current constitution, and meeting records suffice to support its existence and certain role relations within a given window. The researcher has not yet compared out-of-sample performance of grouping by association against modeling continuous activity intensity. These bounded object facts may be reported while ‘this grouping predicts better’ remains unevaluated. Conversely, a comparison failing to support grouping advantage does not justify deleting association records or denying costs already borne by members.

BoundaryThis does not address real registration validity, individual member consent, or responsibility attribution; object facts also remain within their sources' respective scopes.

Uganda's 1996 expenditure tracking: checking objects and funding interfaces stage by stageDocumented case

Reinikka and Svensson's original 2004 journal study uses a 1996 survey of 250 government primary schools to examine 1991–1995 retrospectively. Central, district, and school data were obtained separately. District records showed central incoming funds but lacked reliable school-by-school expenditure records. Table I reports a mean received/entitled ratio of 12.6% for 944 school-year observations, not the share of the entire education budget reaching schools.

SourceReinikka and Svensson, Local Capture: Evidence from a Central Government Transfer Program in UgandaQJE119(2):679–705, May 2004; §III, printed684–685/PDF6–7; Table I, printed687/PDF9, All schools 1991–1995; equation (1) and footnote 6, printed685.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe additional point here is stage-by-stage data collection and object boundaries, not explaining everything through circle labels. The sample excludes private/community and boarding schools. The ratio concerns nonwage capitation grants, with entitlements constructed from 1991 enrollment; it cannot be expanded into a nationwide education-expenditure loss rate. Raw data were not recalculated, personal motives were not adjudicated, and grouping gain was not certified under this book's test requirements.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • This lesson has no complete data or comparison set down in advance for a real candidate circle and therefore grants support to no specific grouping-gain test. Examples support only the listed historical facts; mathematical constructions serve only to explain conditions.

Check your understanding

    Does completing C*'s fifteen items suffice to call it an objective circle?

  2. 2

Does completing C*'s fifteen items suffice to call it an objective circle?

No. These items make claims checkable, but boundaries and internal structure still require corresponding evidence.

Basis: Chinese source lines 2186–2195.

If members do not know one another, must the grouping be only the analyst's imagination?

No. Shared platforms, rules, spaces, or risks may support candidate structures; boundaries and specific relations still require checking.

Basis: Chinese source line 2188.

Without a grouping-gain test, can the existence of a documented school not be recognized?

That inference is invalid. Reliable object facts and grouping-related task gain are different questions.

Basis: Chinese source lines 2130 and 2194, and the structural object (§3.1).

Why is g's test MSE 4 in the example?

Each prediction set down differs from the test target by plus or minus 2; all squared errors are 4, and their mean is 4.

Basis: Teaching construction.

If positive gain fails the positive criterion, can one immediately declare a nongrouped representation fully sufficient?

No. Supporting the null model also requires three predefined criteria: equivalence or sufficiency, power/sensitivity, and tolerance.

Basis: §4.3 and the pre-registration of a formal test.

If evidence is missing on one of the nine axes, should it be deleted or marked not applicable?

Neither should be automatic. Mark insufficient evidence as “unknown”; retain a reasoned “not applicable” only for genuine inapplicability.

Basis: §5.2。

Is a temporary group still the same object after renaming?

It depends on actual conditions such as the identity criterion, membership, and interfaces; neither renaming nor retaining a name settles it alone.

Basis: Chinese source line 2195 and §10.9.

10.2Defining the Joint Object ​

In briefThe definition of the joint object retains which people occupy which positions and which interfaces connect which objects. It does not blend all names into one large agent; it makes local differences, cross-boundary transmission, and unresolved relations visible together.

The multi-circle joint object is written as follows.

MC* = <行动者集合 A，圈层集合 C，圈层关系 Rcc，成员与角色映射 Rac，物质状态 M，体验—意义状态 Ψ，通道与约束 Q，事件流 E，多时钟 T，尺度剖面 SP，证据状态 W，同一性判据 K>.[3]

The value of a joint object lies in preserving local differences and cross-boundary channels. It does not put all related objects into one large circle or assert that a higher-level subject exists. Circles with no identifiable relation may only be observed side by side. If they share only an environment, a direct effect should not be invented. If the relation appears only during an event, it should be recorded as temporary, and the conditions under which it ends should be stated.

Each component of the joint state has something to safeguard and a typical error of its own.

Actor set A: Preserve the states, roles, and privacy boundaries of each actor. The typical error is substituting a circle average for the individual.

Circle set C: Maintain the boundaries, states, and identity of each circle separately. The typical error is merging all background conditions into one overarching circle.

Circle relations Rcc: Record direction, type, delay, threshold, and evidence. The typical error is substituting “interrelated” for a mechanism.

Membership and role mapping Rac: Allow multiple affiliations, role conflicts, and differences in ability to exit. The typical error is assuming that each person belongs to only one circle.

Material state M and experience–meaning state Ψ: Material conditions and experience–meaning conditions are represented side by side. The typical error is material determinism, or reduction to narrative alone.

Channels and constraints Q: Specify the extent and capacity of propagation. The typical error is assuming that impacts are lossless, instantaneous, and reach every position.

Event stream E and multiple clocks T: Record the event stream and the several clocks that are not synchronized. The typical error is updating every state synchronously after each event.

Evidential status W and identity criterion K: Record evidence, unknowns, residuals, and object identity. The typical error is mistaking a complete model for a complete account of reality.

10.2Note

Understanding this section

10.2 Defining the joint object

The definition of the joint object retains which people occupy which positions and which interfaces connect which objects. It does not blend all names into one large agent; it makes local differences, cross-boundary transmission, and unresolved relations visible together.

MC* at Chinese source line 2202 contains twelve items: A, C, Rcc, Rac, M, Ψ, Q, E, T, SP, W, K. It is an interface for a candidate joint representation, not a dynamic equation that predicts merely through symbols. Line 2204 emphasizes ‘preserving local differences and cross-boundary channels’. Joining does not mean flattening differences, much less discovering an agent with unified will above multiple circles. [T-102]

A is the actor set. Preserve task-relevant individual states, roles, and privacy boundaries; the same person appearing in several circles is still one person, not several to add together. Circle averages cannot automatically fill personal states. C is the circle set, each entry retaining its own C*, boundaries, state, and identity support; a large joint boundary cannot replace local verification. [T-102; T-101; T-A]

Rcc records relations among circles: endpoints, direction or explicitly undirected semantics, type, scope, window, and material. State relevant delays and thresholds without inventing numbers for those that do not apply. “The school relates to government” does not specify membership containment, funding allocation, supervision, or information transfer; these edges cannot impersonate each other. Not yet knowing an edge does not establish its absence. [T-102; T-relations]

Rac links actors to circles and roles. One person may execute in a team, provide care in a family, and dissent in a community, with different duties, information, and exit conditions in each position. Membership proves neither actual information transfer nor representative authority. Separating Rcc and Rac reveals both relations between circles not necessarily transmitted through a particular person, and cross-circle membership without any transmission record. [T-102; T-members]

M and Ψ preserve material and experience–meaning conditions respectively. Money, time, bodies, facilities, and actual action capability are not trust, identity, fear, expectations, or value conflicts. The two may interact without one filling the other directly. A recorded transfer does not establish recipient satisfaction; positive evaluation does not establish available resources. Narrow tasks, such as counting equipment, need not force collection of every subjective item. [T-102; T-channels]

Q records channels and constraints: what can travel where, how much, when blocked, and how converted. Rcc gives the relation to be stated; Q develops its operating conditions. They are not two conflicting sets of edges. Information arrival, intelligibility, adoption, and state change occupy different positions; capacity is not actual flow, and an interface does not guarantee immediate lossless receipt by every member. [T-102; T-members; T-feedback]

E is the event stream, preserving event identity, occurrence or report time, and related objects; T contains multiple clocks specifying when variables update. A message may quickly change attention, resources may arrive only on settlement, and organizational rules may take effect through later procedures. An event does not refresh every state to “latest”; untouched variables may also change through their own expiry, recovery, or endogenous processes. [T-102; T-clocks]

The scale profile explicitly belongs to the twelve components. Although this section's item-by-item description combines the other items into eight paragraphs without a separate paragraph for the scale profile, the scale profile cannot be deleted. State the scale profile along all nine axes: aggregation, space, time, organization, causation, observation resolution, influence, network topology, and jurisdiction/authorization. Handle applicability, “unknown”, and a reasoned “not applicable” under §5.2. More circles do not mean broader space, deeper causal explanation, or expanded permission. [T-102; T-SP]

W records evidence status, unknowns, and residuals, tracing each value to source, generation process, and cutoff. The identity criterion K records changes under which object identity persists and must connect with the local circles' identity criteria; joint snapshots cannot swallow local conversions. A filled table shows formal record completeness, not absence of real omissions, complete measurement, or resolution of every conflict. [T-102; T-snapshot; T-change]

Without identifiable circle relations, first observe side by side rather than forcing direct-effect arrows. Here “side-by-side observation” handles insufficient material; it does not automatically establish technical parallel relations, which additionally require absence of containment in the current dimension. If a common environment affects both, draw it pointing separately to each; synchronous change alone cannot become one side driving the other. [T-102; T-parallel; T-causal]

If relations exist only during an event, record their start, ending conditions, and evidence window. Temporary does not mean ineffective or responsibility-free, and ending does not erase past transmission or effects. Conversely, an interface appearing in one crisis is not guaranteed to remain forever or to be assumed always open in subsequent predictions. [T-102; T-temporary; T-change]

The Uganda historical material provides a concrete distinction: recruitment, payroll, daily school decisions, and parental fundraising are different organizational edges. This lesson focuses on their distinct responsibilities and resource relations, rather than repeating the preceding section's funding-arrival proportions. The original cannot support every parent's experience or provide every individual's Rac, so its narrative is not presented as a complete empirical MC* snapshot. [P-UGROLE]

A usable joint representation may be small and explicitly incomplete. The point is not to fill all twelve fields with certainties, but to know what each answers, whose material is missing, and which edges have only candidate grounds. Add relevant information and recheck costs when subsequent questions change; a desire for a fuller model does not justify unlimited personal-data collection. [T-102; T-simple; T-A]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First identify task actors and candidate circles, maintaining local definitions and identity references rather than treating names as established objects.

  2. 2

    State circle relations Rcc separately from memberships/roles Rac, preserving direction, type, scope, window, and evidence.

  3. 3

    Record relevant M and Ψ in parallel and separately develop Q's transmission capacity, conditions, and constraints; do not fill one from the other.

  4. 4

    Use E and T to distinguish events from asynchronous updates; the scale profile specifies the joint representation's position and applicability axis by axis.

  5. 5

    Retain unknowns, disputes, residuals, and object conversions in the evidence status and the identity criterion; a complete set of items does not create real-world completeness.

  6. 6

    Observe side by side without relation material, record common environments separately, and specify ending conditions for temporary relations.

  7. 7

    Use bounded snapshots for subsequent propagation analysis, without inferring unified will, effective feedback, or execution authority from joint representation.

Distinctions to keep clear

A actor set

Preserves individual references and differences.

≠

Circle-membership occurrences

Multiple appearances of one person do not increase the unique headcount.

Rcc circle relations

How two circles connect in a specified dimension.

≠

Rac memberships and roles

Which actor participates in which circle in which role.

Common environment

Common inputs affect several objects separately.

≠

Direct transmission

Requires a specific channel connecting two objects and corresponding evidence.

Channel capacity

The transmission ceiling under the corresponding conditions.

≠

Actual transmission and effects

Need process material and corresponding outcome comparisons.

Joint state

Preserves local-object, relationship, and evidence boundaries.

≠

A higher unified subject

Shared will or concentrated permission cannot thereby be presumed.

Completed table

All responsibility items are recorded.

≠

Complete reality

Unknowns, residuals, and conflicts may remain.

Mathematical teaching construction: overlapping membership and unique headcountTeaching scenario

AssumptionsSets, roles, and values are teaching stipulations with no actual people. The counting unit is unique individuals, not roles or attendances.

Let artificial actor set A={a,b,c}, circles C1={a,b}, C2={b,c}. Their union has size 2+2−1=3, while membership occurrences total 4. Rac may record a executing in C1, b coordinating in C1 and participating in C2, and c executing in C2; Rcc records overlap in the membership dimension. Even if these identities hold, they do not establish that b transferred information from C1 to C2; Q channels and actual E events are needed. A circle mean of 5 also does not imply every person equals 5: (2,8) has the same mean.

BoundaryThe calculation of 3 supports only unique headcount, not voluntary membership, endorsement, effective bridging, or authorization.

Mathematical teaching construction: identical observations, different causal structuresTeaching scenario

AssumptionsEntirely artificial structural-equation models; intervention explicitly replaces only the X equation, leaving all others unchanged, with stipulated probabilities.

Model A gives E equal probabilities of 0 or 1, with X=E, Y=E, and no other source of variation. Model B gives X equal probabilities of 0 or 1 and Y=X. Natural observations in both are only (X,Y)=(0,0) and (1,1), each with probability 1/2. Replacing only X's equation with X=1 in model A leaves Y determined by E, so P(Y=1)=1/2; the same replacement in model B gives Y=1. Synchronization therefore cannot uniquely select common input over direct influence or vice versa.

BoundaryNot a real experiment or estimate of cross-circle causal effects, and no authorization to intervene on real objects.

Teaching construction: a minimal joint record with twelve itemsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe entire record is a teaching stipulation, not a real team snapshot. It illustrates the responsibilities of the items without fabricating completed handoff, authorization, or understanding.

Suppose the task asks only whether two fictional teams complete a file handoff within one day. A lists three artificial actors; C references the definitions of the two teams; Rcc records overlapping membership and a file interface awaiting verification; Rac records participation roles; M records equipment and available work hours; Ψ records task understanding as unknown, without turning hours into attitude; Q records interface capacity and permission as pending checks; E records planned submission as a plan; T separates submission and confirmation times; SP lists task scope axis by axis, marking missing material as “unknown”; W lists stipulated values and absent real material; K identifies teams under the stipulated team definitions within this window, requiring reconstruction if roles/interfaces fundamentally change.

BoundaryActual values for the axes of the scale profile are not provided, so this is not a complete case directly usable for real prediction; unknowns are honestly retained, not automatically zero-filled.

Ugandan primary schools' multiple responsibility relations cannot become one superior–subordinate edgeDocumented case

Reinikka and Svensson describe the 1991–1995 institutional setting: teachers were recruited at district level while central government maintained payroll; school parent-teacher associations participated in major decisions, and parental funding was another source. Recruitment, payroll, school decisions, and resource inputs therefore need separate tracing.

SourceReinikka and Svensson, Local Capture (2004)§II Institutional Setting, printed pp.682–684/PDF pp.4–6; teacher-recruitment/central-payroll passages and PTA description.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis section adds relation types and role responsibilities rather than repeating funding proportions. Limited to the historical setting described, without extrapolation to all current schools. It invents no individual parent's experience, every teacher's choice, or complete Rac, and certifies no predictive advantage of the joint model.

If each of two circles has two members, may their total be called four people?

First check overlap. The example shares b, so unique headcount is 3; only role occurrences total 4.

Basis: Set inclusion-exclusion calculation.

If b belongs to both circles, may one determine that information has been bridged?

No. Identity supplies only a possible interface; actual transmission and results need event and channel material separately.

Basis: §10.5 and the teaching example.

If two circles change together, which two explanations should first be distinguished?

A common input affecting each side versus actual transmission between them; synchronization alone cannot distinguish these.

Basis: Chinese source line 2204 and the structural-equation counterexample.

Why does Y remain 0 half the time after do(X=1) in model A?

The intervention replaces only X's equation; Y=E stays unchanged, and E remains equally likely 0/1.

Basis: The artificial model's explicit intervention semantics.

If the source's item-by-item description has no separate paragraph on the scale profile, may scale be omitted?

No. The scale profile is listed explicitly among the twelve components, and the rule of stating it axis by axis along the nine axes still applies.

Basis: Chinese source line 2202 and §5.2.

After an event, must every untouched variable retain its original value?

Not necessarily. They may change through endogenous processes, recovery, or expiry rules; without grounds, retain the last observation with uncertainty or mark unknown.

Basis: §10.7。

May a joint record replace individual states with circle averages?

No automatic replacement. Individual differences and privacy remain; the task determines where averages apply.

Basis: This section's item for the set of actors A.

10.3Six Kinds of Circle Relation ​

In briefThe six relations answer different questions and can overlap; do not force a single choice among six.

The six kinds of relation are six starting points for description, used to distinguish different questions. They are nonexclusive, address different dimensions, and do not exhaust real-world relations. Parallelism, nesting, and overlap describe positions along a specified dimension. Bridging and competition describe connections or constraints. Temporariness describes duration and conditions for ending. These descriptions can be combined. For each actual circle relation, state separately the source circle, target circle, direction, shared members or interfaces, channel, extent, time window, and relevant evidence. Do not force a value for a delay or threshold that does not apply.

10.3Note

Understanding this section

10.3 Six kinds of circle relation

The six relations answer different questions and can overlap; do not force a single choice among six.

The source begins: “They are nonexclusive, address different dimensions, and do not exhaust real-world relations.” Positional relations, connections and constraints, and persistence are different observational dimensions. Asking who contains whom and whether two sides compete for resources need not have only one answer; asking whether a relation is temporary does not cancel membership overlap. Read the six sections separately, then combine them into qualified relation records. [T-10.3]

Parallel, nested, and overlapping first specify the membership, operating-arrangement, role, resource, or spatial basis of comparison. Bridging identifies an interface, with actual transmission and outcomes separately verified; competition requires one side to change the other's available set; temporary relations must distinguish a limited task duration from merely short-term evidence. These words are neither ranked levels nor stages automatically progressing from parallel relations to institutionalization. [T-10.3; T-cross]

Each relationship needs a source circle, target circle, direction, common members or interface, channel, scope, window, and evidence. Set overlap can usually be recorded as symmetric; funding transfers may be directional, and flows in both directions should be separated. Fill delays and thresholds only when they have a valid meaning for that relationship and question; do not invent a ‘transmission speed’ for a membership intersection. Missing data and inapplicability must also remain distinct. [T-10.3；T-missing]

The parent section supplies the classification grammar, while 10.3.1—10.3.6 each provide criteria for one of six entry points. The final subsection's table returns to the whole, listing checks and failure or conversion for every relationship; this does not subordinate the other five types to temporary relationships. The website preserves the final subsection's complete original-text location while this explanation clarifies the table's function across sections. [T-10.3；T-10.3.6]

The strongest objection is that multiple labels could explain anything. The response is not to add labels but to fix dimensions, endpoints, observation windows, and failure conditions. Membership containment must be revised if members outside the boundary are found; knowing only that both sides know the same person cannot establish effective bridging transmission. Permitting labels to coexist does not exempt them from evidence. [T-cross；T-object]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First fix the two candidate objects and the relationship dimension in question.

  2. 2

    Check position, channels, constraints, and persistence separately for the different questions.

  3. 3

    State traceable materials and failure cases for each judgment.

  4. 4

    Combine only grounded labels; do not infer causal strength or shared will from the number of relationships.

Distinctions to keep clear

Multidimensional classification

Different questions may hold simultaneously.

≠

Mutually exclusive classification

Each object belongs to only one category; this text explicitly does not adopt that approach.

Nonexhaustive

Domain relationships not described by the six types may be retained.

≠

Arbitrary labeling

The criteria for each type cannot be omitted.

Teaching construction: recording three dimensions simultaneouslyTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe sets, deadline, and sole device are assumptions, not facts about an actual project.

Let project A have members {a,b} and department B members {b,c}, with A's task due Friday; both need the sole device during the same period. Membership overlaps without either containing the other; the deadline makes A temporary by prior designation; if A's use of the device excludes B, competition exists in that window. Removing the shared-device constraint removes only competition, not membership overlap or the deadline.

BoundaryArtificial stipulations test definitions and inferences; they are not actual events, measurement results, or evidence of framework effectiveness.

Yes. Duration and membership position answer different questions and cannot replace one another.

If none of the six types fits, must the nearest one be forced onto the case?

No. Retain the specific domain relationship or unknown, explaining which question the six types do not cover.

Basis: The source does not claim to exhaust reality.

10.3　六类圈层关系; Chinese source lines 2224–2227; SHA-256 0d9e445bcba84380a572d248dad4836013b735d7d33589f29ea0c6f1aeb61c10

  • The current source section and this text’s conceptual explanation of v3.0; not a substitute for external empirical materials.
  • Older research attachments retain their original manuscript identity; the previous scope of external reading has not expanded because of this edition change.

10.3.1Parallelism ​

In briefParallel means absence of the currently declared containment relationship, not absence of connections.

Parallelism means that, under the current definition, the circles have no relation of containment in either membership or operating arrangements. Parallel circles may still be related. Two parallel teams may share a budget, a platform, and higher-level institutional arrangements. They may also be triggered simultaneously by the same event. If only shared exposure can be confirmed, record a shared environment. Record cross-circle propagation only when a channel for information, resources, personnel, or institutional write-back (§7.1) has been found.

10.3.1Note

Understanding this section

10.3.1 Parallel

Parallel means absence of the currently declared containment relationship, not absence of connections.

The source says: ‘the circles have no relation of containment in either membership or operating arrangements’. ‘Parallel’ is first a negative positional judgment relative to the current definition, not something established merely because an organizational chart places items on the same horizontal row. Specify which membership or operating-arrangement relations were checked; unknown is not proven absence of containment. [T-10.3.1]

Two teams can have separate tasks and boundaries while sharing budgets, platforms, or higher-level institutions. Thus ‘the same superior’ does not imply one team contains the other, and parallelism guarantees neither independence nor lack of interference. For common exposure, first create a shared-environment node to avoid drawing synchronous change as A driving B. [T-10.3.1；T-causal]

When cross-team interfaces for messages, resources, personnel, or write-back are found, the parallel positional judgment may remain while bridging or transmission is recorded separately. An information interface concerns what relationship exists; a specified effect concerns whether that interface changes the target. These involve different levels of evidence collection. Failure to find a direct channel does not exclude a common cause. [T-10.3.1；T-members]

The table's indication that ‘overlap or bridging appears’ should mean that relationship records need updating or additional dimensions, not that parallelism must be revoked. The body text declares the six types nonexclusive; only if the original parallel claim also asserted complete separation of membership would a new intersection refute that stronger hypothesis. [T-10.3；T-10.3.6]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Specify the compared objects and membership/operating-arrangement basis.

  2. 2

    Check for containment, without substituting a common superior.

  3. 3

    For synchronous changes, first compare common environments with direct channels.

  4. 4

    New bridging materials update only the relationship assertions actually changed.

Distinctions to keep clear

Parallel

No containment along the currently declared dimension.

≠

Independent

Statistical or causal independence requires separate evidence.

Common exposure

An external condition reaches both sides simultaneously.

≠

A transmits to B

Requires evidence of a path from A to B.

Teaching construction: common input without a direct edgeTeaching scenario

AssumptionsFixed equations; the operation changing only X alters neither E nor the Y equation.

Let team outputs be X=10−E and Y=20−2E, with artificial shock E equal to 0 or 1. At E=1 both decline simultaneously, but the equations contain neither X→Y nor Y→X. Changing only X while holding E fixed leaves Y unchanged. Matching temporal direction cannot supply direct transmission; this is a counterexample in an explicitly stipulated model, not an actual estimate.

BoundaryArtificial stipulations test definitions and inferences; they are not actual events, measurement results, or evidence of framework effectiveness.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • No reader test was conducted; actual-object classifications, channel effects, and authority require independent checks against their respective materials.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If two teams reduce output simultaneously, may mutual transmission be claimed?

  2. 2

    If a bridging edge is established while absence of containment still holds, may parallelism remain?

If two teams reduce output simultaneously, may mutual transmission be claimed?

No; distinguish common shocks, selection, and actual transmission.

Basis: A shared environment is not cross-circle transmission.

If a bridging edge is established while absence of containment still holds, may parallelism remain?

Yes. State that positions remain parallel while bridging exists, rather than forcing a choice of one of six types.

Basis: The parent section's nonexclusivity qualification.

10.3.2Nesting ​

In briefNesting must specify whether the containment concerns members, roles, accounting, jurisdiction, or space.

Nesting means that one object’s extent is actually contained within another along an explicitly specified relational dimension. The basis of containment must be stated. Membership, roles, resource accounting, institutional jurisdiction, and space are distinct dimensions. If the claim concerns containment of only a part, first identify the contained subobject and its boundary. If two sets intersect but neither contains the other, record overlap on that dimension. Describing the intersection as “partial containment” does not also justify classifying it as nesting. A subcircle’s state cannot directly represent the higher-level circle, and the outer circle’s rules need not take effect in the same way at every position inside it.

10.3.2Note

Understanding this section

10.3.2 Nested

Nesting must specify whether the containment concerns members, roles, accounting, jurisdiction, or space.

The source requires an ‘explicit relational dimension’ (translated from Chinese). Containment of a membership set means every member lies in the larger set; including budgets in one accounting scope is another kind of containment; location within an administrative jurisdiction also does not automatically imply organizational subordination. One containment cannot be arbitrarily copied to other dimensions. [T-10.3.2；T-SP]

If only a part is contained, first name that part as a bounded subobject, then check its containment relationship. If the two original sets only intersect and neither fully contains the other, record overlap. Treating ‘partial containment’ as full nesting conceals members outside the boundary, distinct authority, or portions with other interfaces. [T-10.3.2]

A subcircle's state cannot directly represent the upper level. High load in one team does not mean every position in the whole institution is overloaded; existence of a higher-level rule also does not mean it is implemented at every inner level. Upward aggregation must retain distributions, while downward constraints require interface-by-interface checks of effect, exceptions, and offsets. [T-10.3.2；T-cross]

The larger circle in the diagram expresses only the declared dimension, conferring neither higher value nor comprehensive authority to act. Organizational containment does not automatically expand the scope of jurisdiction and authorization; using a superior's authority over one matter for another action requires separate valid grounds covering that object and action. [T-SP]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Fix one comparable dimension.

  2. 2

    Check item by item whether the entire source scope lies within the target scope.

  3. 3

    If only part qualifies, create a subobject rather than calling the original object wholly contained.

  4. 4

    Separately check aggregation losses, downward rule transmission, and matter-specific authority.

Distinctions to keep clear

Membership containment

All members satisfy the target boundary.

≠

Spatial containment

A location lies within the scope without automatically changing membership or organizational affiliation.

Nested

Actual containment under the specified basis.

≠

Overlapping

An intersection exists, but neither fully contains the other.

Teaching construction: subobjects and whole-object containmentTeaching scenario

AssumptionsFinite artificial sets; the strict-containment symbol ⊂ denotes a proper subset.

A={a,b} and B={b,c,d}. A∩B={b}, but a is not in B and c is not in A, so the two original sets overlap. If the shared members within A are specifically studied as S={b}, then S⊂B and S⊂A hold. This true proposition about a subobject cannot be rewritten as A⊂B.

BoundaryArtificial stipulations test definitions and inferences; they are not actual events, measurement results, or evidence of framework effectiveness.

No. Space and organization are different bases.

It is a new, narrower object judgment and cannot establish containment of the entire source circle.

10.3.3Overlap ​

In briefOverlap retains specific shared items; a ratio cannot tell us who bears what.

Overlap means that circles share some members, roles, resources, or interfaces without fully containing one another. Positions of overlap may take on bridging, translation, and coordination. They may also face role conflict, conflicting loyalties, duplicated work, and risks of information leakage. The proportion of overlap cannot substitute for a record of what is actually shared.

10.3.3Note

Understanding this section

10.3.3 Overlapping

Overlap retains specific shared items; a ratio cannot tell us who bears what.

The source says: ‘circles share some members, roles, resources, or interfaces without fully containing one another’. Overlap first fixes the same basis of comparison, then identifies the intersection and items unique to each side. Sharing a venue does not automatically establish shared membership; the same designation also does not replace identity checks for the same person, resource, or interface. [T-10.3.3]

Overlapping positions may facilitate translation, coordination, and bridging, or bear conflicts, duplicate work, and leakage risks. ‘May’ does not mean every shared member faces conflicting loyalties; check specific tasks, information visibility, confidentiality requirements, work hours, and refusal conditions. A roster cannot establish inner states. [T-10.3.3；T-members]

A ratio describes only the degree of commonality under a given denominator. For example, the intersection can simultaneously comprise half of A and a quarter of B; omitting denominators makes the same relationship appear inconsistent. Two networks with the same ratio may share different key roles, so capacity and transmission effects remain unknown. [T-10.3.3]

Member counts must be deduplicated, while role occurrences may be counted separately. Unique persons, participation counts, work hours, and authorized shares are different quantities; a common member cannot be counted as two people while their limited time is assumed to provide two capacities. [T-members；T-joint]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    List shared and unique items for the two circles separately.

  2. 2

    Check shared-item identities and the observation window.

  3. 3

    State ratio denominators; do not substitute a ratio for specific shared positions.

  4. 4

    Collect evidence separately for bridging effects, duplicate burdens, and information risks.

Distinctions to keep clear

Shared member

The same person appears in two membership sets.

≠

Authorized representative

Requires grounds covering the matter and scope.

Overlap ratio

A set quantity under the specified denominator.

≠

Key shared item

Determines which resource, responsibility, or information is connected.

Teaching construction: deduplicated headcount and capacityTeaching scenario

AssumptionsOne shared person, commensurate work hours, the same day, and mutually exclusive tasks; all numbers are teaching stipulations.

A={a,b,c}, B={c,d,e}, with intersection {c}. Unique headcount=3+3−1=5, while membership occurrences=6. If c has only 4 hours that day and each side requires 3 hours, the total demand of 6 hours exceeds 4, leaving a 2-hour gap. That gap follows only if tasks occupy the same window and cannot be performed simultaneously; membership overlap alone cannot imply overload.

BoundaryArtificial stipulations test definitions and inferences; they are not actual events, measurement results, or evidence of framework effectiveness.

If the overlap ratio is 1/3 in both A and B, is that sufficient to judge who is most important?

No. The shared item's role, tasks, and substitution conditions are needed.

Basis: A ratio does not replace specific shared items.

If both sides require 3 hours from a shared person, must there be a 2-hour gap?

Only if assumptions such as 4 actually available hours, the same window, and nonparallel tasks hold.

Basis: Capacity premises of the teaching construction.

10.3.4Bridging ​

In briefBridging requires an identifiable interface; successful transmission is not authority to represent.

Bridging means that an actor, institution, interface, text, platform, or event connects previously separate circles. A bridging party need not have authority to represent others or be loyal to either side. For any bridge, transmission capability, translation losses, selective filtering, responsibility, substitutability, overload, and exit conditions must be stated separately.

10.3.4Note

Understanding this section

10.3.4 Bridging

Bridging requires an identifiable interface; successful transmission is not authority to represent.

The original lists actors, institutions, interfaces, texts, platforms, and events as possible bridging carriers. A bridge need not be a person, and mere ‘relatedness’ between sides does not establish it. At minimum specify source, target, the content transmitted, interface, and window, and whether the material supports only potential capability or an actual transmission record. [T-10.3.4; T-members]

Transmission capability, transmission occurring, and transmission causing an outcome differ. A bilingual member may be able to translate without participating in this case; delivered email may establish transmission without changed beliefs; understanding also implies neither agreement nor execution. Effect claims still need comparisons and channel evidence; bridge position or centrality cannot substitute. [T-members; T-causal]

Explain translation loss, filtering, responsibility, substitutes, overload, and exit individually. A summary may correctly preserve the current task answer or collapse critical distinctions; neither loss nor losslessness can be universally declared. A backup bridge sharing the same blocked information source may not substitute. Bridge actors’ limited time and refusal conditions are real constraints on sustained mechanism operation. [T-10.3.4; T-cross]

Neither representative authority nor loyalty follows from bridge position. Translating A’s words does not authorize signing a contract for A; carrying documents for both sides does not establish shared values with either. Classify responsibility by actual conduct, authority, and specific grounds, without automatically assigning all consequences to the bridge actor. [T-10.3.4; T-authority]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Identify endpoints, the content transmitted, and connecting interface.

  2. 2

    Check available capability, actual transmission, and outcomes separately.

  3. 3

    Check filtering, task loss, capacity, substitutes, and exit.

  4. 4

    Check representative authority and responsibility separately; network position creates no power.

Distinctions to keep clear

Transmission capability

An interface can transmit under conditions.

≠

Transmission effect

The specified target has changed, requiring independent material.

Translation

Rewrites the content transmitted into another expression.

≠

Representation on behalf

Making valid decisions for others, with separate authorization requirements.

Teaching construction: three steps cannot be compressed into oneTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAn artificial file process, without actual accounts, communications, or permission changes.

Suppose A sends B a file and the platform records delivery, but B cannot read it without decryption permission. Network delivery is established; understanding is unknown and currently blocked; changed action is unproved. Valid decryption permission and confirmed reading may update understanding material; adoption and changed outcomes still need separate checks.

BoundaryArtificial stipulations test definitions and inferences; they are not actual events, measurement results, or evidence of framework effectiveness.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Does relaying someone’s original words authorize signing for them?

  2. 2

    Does B’s inaction mean the message did not arrive?

Does relaying someone’s original words authorize signing for them?

No. Transmission of expression creates no representative authorization.

Basis: A bridge actor need not have representative authority.

Does B’s inaction mean the message did not arrive?

Not necessarily; the message may arrive and even be understood without adoption.

Basis: Separate transmission, understanding, and action.

10.3.5Competition ​

In briefCompetition requires exclusionary constraints on available sets; different goals alone are insufficient.

Competition means that circles create identifiable exclusionary constraints on scarce resources, attention, legitimacy, member commitments, interpretive authority, or room for action. Different goals do not automatically amount to competition. Record competition only when one circle’s use of what is available, its rules, or its actions changes the set available to another circle. Cooperation and competition can coexist through different channels.

10.3.5Note

Understanding this section

10.3.5 Competition

Competition requires exclusionary constraints on available sets; different goals alone are insufficient.

The original lists scarce resources, attention, legitimacy, member commitments, interpretive authority, and room for action. These cannot all be compressed into one currency or energy, but share the question whether A’s occupation, rules, or actions change B’s actual available set. Different needs without mutual exclusion establish difference, not directly competition. [T-10.3.5]

First specify resource type, window, capacity, and exclusion rule. One person doing A’s task in the morning and B’s in the evening need not face competition within the same window; equipment unavailable to B during A’s reserved period creates an exclusion constraint in that window. Interpretive authority or eligibility may also matter and needs specific rules, not unsupported speculation about hostility. [T-10.3.5; T-joint]

Cooperation and competition may coexist: sharing safety information reduces accident risk while the same-period test equipment is contested. Resource competition does not cancel cooperation, nor does cooperation prove fully aligned interests. Expanding capacity, staggering times, or creating sharing rules may change feasible sets, but ‘communication’ cannot remove every competition. [T-10.3.5]

The NASA report consulted here records prioritization of testing and analysis but does not give detailed exclusive occupation of a scarce resource between two teams on the checked pages. It is used only as an actual boundary case of ‘scheduling exists, competition remains unproved’, without inventing team conflict, resource grabbing, or competition-caused accidents. Formal examples can explicitly show when competition holds. [P-10.3.5]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Fix what is contested, same-type units, and time window.

  2. 2

    Compare whether B’s available set shrinks when A occupies the resource.

  3. 3

    Exclude vague labels based only on different goals or shared scarcity.

  4. 4

    State cooperative and competitive channels separately; propose conditions relieving constraints, not promised effects.

Distinctions to keep clear

Different goals

The sides desire different endpoints.

≠

Competition

One side changes the other’s feasible set.

Scarcity

Demand is constrained relative to available quantity.

≠

Hostility

Subjective malice cannot be inferred automatically from scarcity or exclusion.

Teaching construction: capacity one and joint schedulingTeaching scenario

AssumptionsSame-type indivisible tests, no parallel execution, and one deadline; no actual allocation authority is granted.

The only test bench can perform one complete test in the morning; A and B each need one, both due that morning. Let a,b∈{0,1}, with feasible constraint a+b≤1. Once A occupies it with a=1, B’s available set changes from {0,1} to {0}. Raising concurrent capacity to 2 changes the constraint to a+b≤2 and permits both. Adding capacity only in the afternoon while preserving the deadline still fails the original joint target.

BoundaryArtificial stipulations test definitions and inferences; they are not actual events, measurement results, or evidence of framework effectiveness.

10.3.6Temporariness ​

In briefTemporary may mean a predetermined limited duration or merely support within a short window; the two must not be conflated.

Temporary circles form around events, tasks, crises, shared exposure, or short-term goals. They may dissolve rapidly or become more durable through traces, stabilization of roles, and institutionalization. Calling a circle “temporary” may follow from a task deadline set in advance or be a provisional judgment based on the short time window observed so far. The two cases should be distinguished. A temporary relation can be important, carry responsibilities, and already be real. A temporary alliance can still overlap in membership, compete for resources, and be bridged through particular interfaces.

RelationMinimum CriterionWhat to Check in ParticularFailure or Change
ParallelismNo containment relation at presentShared environment and indirect couplingContainment, overlap, or bridging emerges
NestingExplicit containment in membership, operating arrangements, jurisdiction, or spaceDownward constraints and loss from upward aggregationThe identity criterion changes, exit occurs, or jurisdiction is reconfigured
OverlapSome members, roles, resources, or interfaces are sharedRole conflict and double countingShared items disappear or the relation becomes containment
BridgingIdentifiable interface for cross-circle transmissionTranslation, filtering, overload, and authority to representThe channel closes, is replaced, or becomes institutionalized
CompetitionAn exclusionary constraint on the available setScarce items, time window, and channels for cooperationResources expand, rules are coordinated, or a party exits
TemporarinessA clearly finite duration, or support so far limited to a short time window. Distinguish the twoEnding, traces, and who takes up responsibility. Temporariness can be combined with other dimensions of relationThe temporary relation ends, is extended, or becomes institutionalized. Its positions and channel relations are recorded separately

“Change” in the table records a shift in a relation’s type or defining conditions between the states before and after an event. Referring back to the relation by the same name does not by itself establish that it has changed. Relations can persist, strengthen, weaken, change direction, change type, or dissolve. Every such judgment must be tied to snapshots before and after, the dimension that changed, and object identity.

10.3.6Note

Understanding this section

10.3.6 Temporary

Temporary may mean a predetermined limited duration or merely support within a short window; the two must not be conflated.

The original lists events, tasks, crises, shared exposures, and short-term goals as entry points for temporary circles. The first ‘temporary’ comes from an end agreed in advance for the task; the second from having observed only a brief interval, with future persistence unknown. Short observation does not establish imminent disappearance, and task expiry does not automatically establish that actual activity ended. [T-10.3.6]

Temporary does not mean unimportant, without responsibility, or without actual relationships. An event coalition can have members, resources, and commitments while overlapping, competing, and bridging in different dimensions. Its end does not erase duties to preserve evidence, settle costs, or provide later remedies; who bears them needs specific rules. Neither ‘temporary’ nor ‘left traces’ directly distributes unlimited obligations. [T-10.3.6; T-exit]

Moving from short-term to lasting requires at least checking how traces persist, roles repeat, and institutional rules enter actual operation. Leaving an archive is not forming a permanent institution; announcing a permanent name is not continuity of personnel, resources, and processes. If the identity criterion fails, record object conversion or dissolution rather than merely carrying the old record forward. [T-10.3.6; T-change]

This section’s table reviews six relations: parallel checks shared environments and indirect coupling; nesting checks downward constraints and upward aggregation loss; overlap checks role conflict and double counting; bridging checks translation, filtering, overload, and representative authority; competition checks scarce items, windows, and cooperative channels; temporary checks ending, traces, and responsibility uptake. ‘Failure or transformation’ is a set of entry points for checks, not a declaration that every relation must follow that path. [T-10.3.6]

The final paragraph distinguishes maintenance, strengthening, weakening, redirection, type change, and dissolution. Give before-and-after snapshots, changed dimensions, and the identity criterion before naming the change. Increased flow may be only a capacity change in the same bridge, not a type change; completing a scheduled task may close only an interface without dissolving original member organizations. [T-10.3.6]

The NASA case establishes only a task-based investigation arrangement after the accident with a duty to produce a final report. Checked material does not establish a specific dissolution date or settlement of all later obligations. It illustrates that task and evidence windows should be stated separately; report completion cannot directly become ‘benign exit fully completed’. [P-10.3.6]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Determine whether temporary means an agreed duration or short-window material.

  2. 2

    Record evidence of formation, activity, extension, and actual ending separately.

  3. 3

    Check continuity of traces, resources, roles, and responsibilities.

  4. 4

    Compare relations and the identity criterion before and after, classify bounded changes, and do not rename retrospectively to conceal history.

Distinctions to keep clear

Predetermined duration

The arrangement states when or under what conditions it ends.

≠

Short-window support

Only the observed window is known; future persistence is unknown.

Task completion

This work reaches its agreed endpoint.

≠

All responsibilities settled

Requires additional residual-obligation and uptake material.

Teaching construction: three date cardsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll dates are relative-day teaching assumptions, with no actual group or statutory deadline.

A fictional group’s task arrangement schedules task completion for day 7, while records cover only days 1–3. The scheduled duration is known to be 7 days, but actual stopping on day 7 remains unknown. If lawfully extended on day 6 to day 14, preserve the original deadline and extension version. If the task ends on day 7 but custody of records lacks continuity, record task ending and settlement of responsibility separately.

BoundaryArtificial stipulations test definitions and inferences; they are not actual events, measurement results, or evidence of framework effectiveness.
