If removing a circle leaves prediction unchanged, may facts about its affected members be deleted?

No. Predictive gain and independent object/responsibility facts concern different questions; simplify the prediction model while preserving necessary records.

Basis: §10.1、§10.10。

What if a conclusion holds only in a very narrow time window?

State the window and sensitivity without extrapolating to other periods; check whether the relation is genuinely temporary during the event.

Basis: Time perturbation.

Does a new institution automatically remove the old institution's responsibilities?

A new-object label cannot imply this; retain history and check responsibilities matter by matter.

Basis: This section's final sentence.

10.10The Complexity Check for Joint States ​

In briefAn added layer of explanation must state which additional question it answers. Better prediction needs comparison; real responsibilities need preservation without predictive scores proving their existence.

Adding circles increases the ability to fit the data and also increases error, data requirements, and degrees of freedom in explanation. Each added circle or relation must be assessed on which residual in the original model it explains, whether it has an independently observable channel, and whether it improves out-of-sample explanation or foresight. Its measurement costs and privacy risks must also be specified, and the conclusion checked with that circle or relation removed.

Multi-circle models must be compared with a simple single-focus or single-circle baseline. If a gain in prediction or explanation is claimed but the complex model only tells a fuller story about the materials already observed, without stable comparative support, downgrade the claim of gain and prefer an adequate simpler model. Keeping an object to describe established responsibilities, differences among members, or lawful permissions need not first establish a predictive gain. The independent question it answers should still be stated, recording costs should be controlled, and more data should not be treated as better explanation. Complexity does not amount to maturity. Using one fewer circle is usually better if no important distinction is lost.

10.10Note

Understanding this section

10.10 The complexity check for joint states

An added layer of explanation must state which additional question it answers. Better prediction needs comparison; real responsibilities need preservation without predictive scores proving their existence.

The source's concise conclusion is, in translation, “Complexity is not maturity.” Adding circles or relations adds representational freedom, parameters, error sources, and data needs; better storytelling may merely fit already-seen material better. This does not prove complex models necessarily worse; it makes extra complexity a choice requiring explanation rather than a default reward. [T-main]

Answer five questions individually: which residual of the original model it explains, preventing aimless expansion; whether an independently observable channel exists, preventing label-only links; whether it improves out-of-sample explanation or foresight, preventing circular explanation of old material; what measurement costs and privacy risks arise, preventing losses exceeding gains; and whether deleting it changes the conclusion, checking duplication. The last tests task contribution; any numerical change after deletion does not automatically prove usefulness. [T-main]

Against a simple single-focus or single-circle baseline, both must answer the same target using comparable cutoffs, samples, and evaluation methods. A complex option cannot exclusively use later-known outcomes or extra labels and credit the difference to structure. Out-of-sample explanation also needs predefined targets and failures; explaining any new material afterward is not automatically support. Numerical prediction, mechanism explanation, and normative description still have different evidential responsibilities. [T-main; T-entry]

If there is only a complete narrative within already seen materials and no stable comparative support, lower the claimed explanatory or predictive gain and prefer a sufficiently simple model. Stable comparison may be bounded to specific tasks and intervals and does not require every new case to collect a large independent training set; when adequate comparison is infeasible, honestly retain gain as unestablished rather than claiming validation. [T-main]

The source preserves a key exception: describing established responsibilities, membership differences, or lawful authority can independently justify retaining an object without first proving predictive gain. For example, two people may have the same average income but different care obligations; describing those responsibilities is not intended to improve prediction of tomorrow's returns. The exception still requires independent grounds, an explicit question, and cost control; ‘responsibility matters’ cannot justify unlimited collection of everyone's private information. [T-main]

The added point from the NASA report here concerns the use of duty records themselves: the board and Panel 1 each had explicit tasks. If the question tracks who was required to investigate and report, documentary reasons justify retaining those levels without first proving improved prediction. Conversely, duties written in documents still establish neither performance effects nor optimality of that organizational configuration. [P-NASA]

The strongest objection is that simple baselines flatten weak positions. The right response is to clarify the target rather than abandon the baseline: if the original task includes membership differences or responsibility, a ‘simple model’ deleting them no longer answers the same question. Sufficient simplicity must preserve key distinctions; complexity and simplicity should concern sufficiency rather than a contest in object counts. [T-main；T-snapshot]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    State the current question, simple baseline, and its residuals or unanswered matters.

  2. 2

    For each added circle, explain its channel, task contribution, costs, and privacy implications.

  3. 3

    When claiming gains, make fair independent/out-of-sample comparisons, retaining failures and uncertainty.

  4. 4

    If only an in-sample narrative is obtained, lower the gain claim without automatically denying object facts.

  5. 5

    If retaining complexity for responsibility or authority records, explain its independent grounds and stopping scope.

Distinctions to keep clear

More materials

More records or dimensions.

≠

Better explanation

Testable gain on the same task, not merely greater length.

Predictive use

Compare performance on unseen outcomes.

≠

Responsibility-description use

Retain established duties and parties; predictive scores do not certify their existence.

Sufficiently simple

Key questions and distinctions are still answered.

≠

Arbitrary omission

Deleting task-essential objects has changed the question.

Mathematical teaching construction: lower training error, higher unseen errorTeaching scenario

AssumptionsTraining and test data are entirely artificial, assessed under the same squared loss, with the test value unused in fitting; no claim is made to represent an actual probability distribution.

Artificial training points are (x,y)=(0,0),(1,1). The simple constant prediction m=0.5 has training mean squared error [(0−0.5)^2+(1−0.5)^2]/2=0.25; the two-parameter line y=x has zero training error. Add a test point (2,0) not used for fitting: the constant has squared error 0.25, while the line has (0−2)^2=4. This example refutes only ‘better training performance necessarily means better unseen performance’; under a different actual generating law, the line could win.

BoundaryThis is a logical counterexample, not an estimate of how often multi-circle models win or lose; one test point also supplies no stable empirical conclusion.

Teaching construction: deleting a responsibility item with no predictive contributionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsEntirely artificial, with the failure function and authorization facts given separately; no actual shutdown occurred.

An artificial model predicts tomorrow's equipment failure using only equipment measurements; adding an authorized-duty-personnel roster leaves prediction unchanged. The roster may be removed from that predictive model, but if the task also asks who may stop the equipment, grounded authorization records remain necessary. The uses require different sufficient summaries; no predictive gain does not waive authority checks.

BoundaryPreserving permission records does not mean permission to act has been obtained; execution still requires checking the specific matter.

Apollo 13 investigation duties: record value is not certified by predictive scoresDocumented case

The 1970 investigation report's terms of reference and panel-duty pages separately state the board's investigation/reporting duties and Panel 1's tasks. Organizational distinctions have an independent use when tracing these documentary responsibilities.

Does a complex model providing more detail directly count as explanatory gain?

No. Ask about independent support and comparative performance on the same task.

Basis: The complexity check.

Must an object with no predictive gain but formal duty documents be deleted?

Not necessarily. It may be retained to trace duties, with its use and cost explained and no false claim of predictive gain.

Basis: This section's qualification.

If a simple model becomes more accurate after deleting affected people, is it sufficient?

If the original task requires their protection or differences, the model has failed to answer part of it; average accuracy alone cannot decide.

Basis: Sufficiency depends on the task.

10.11An Example of a Joint Object ​

In briefThis section uses a public resignation to connect the preceding items. Its focus is preserving potentially different relationships, resources, meanings, and times, then letting evidence determine which paths hold.

An analysis of an employee’s public departure from a job can identify the actor, project team, company management, family care circle, professional community, and public opinion on a platform at the same time. The team is nested within the company. The employee belongs to the overlapping team, family, and professional circles. The platform bridges the employee and the public outside the company. The team and management may compete over resource allocation but cooperate in maintaining reputation. A group that forms around the departure to express support may be a temporary circle.

Material conditions include pay, working hours, care, contracts, job positions, and platform traffic. Experience–meaning conditions include dignity, a sense of betrayal, professional identity, trust in coworkers, and perceived legitimacy among the public. The departure immediately changes attention and emotion, then affects trust and handover in the team. Organizational processes may change weeks later, and institutional rules may be written back later still. Any single-track explanation that the person “left because of their personality” or that the departure was “entirely determined by company structure” must be compared with the joint state.

The snapshot makes different paths visible. If the company responds only through public relations without changing working hours or appeal channels, emotions on the platform may subside while internal distrust persists. If resources are adjusted but repair of meaning fails, people may stay while their commitments continue to weaken. If the pressure of family care is lifted, the actor’s available options change. If the professional community provides resources through a bridge, the cost of exit decreases and others may follow the example. The next Part uses event-driven projection to examine which path the evidence supports.

10.11Note

Understanding this section

10.11 A joint-object example

This section uses a public resignation to connect the preceding items. Its focus is preserving potentially different relationships, resources, meanings, and times, then letting evidence determine which paths hold.

The source is not an investigation record of a company but an example of ‘an analysis of an employee’s public departure from a job’. The agent, team, management, household care, occupational community, and platform public discourse may all be candidates; listing them in a sentence does not give them object admission. An actual case must find boundary, role, channel, time, and identity materials item by item; household conditions or personal feelings lacking materials cannot be invented. [T-main；T-entry]

The relationship layer retains, in turn, the team's local nesting within the company, the agent's multiple memberships, platform bridging to external audiences, the distinct relations of resource competition and reputational cooperation, and the temporary nature of solidarity circles during the event. Management need not equal the entire company, and employee and family are not the same agent. A platform may spread messages without representing either side; ‘possible competition/cooperation’ is also not factual confirmation. [T-main；T-rel]

The M side lists pay, work hours, care, contracts, positions, and traffic; the Ψ side lists dignity, feelings of betrayal, professional identity, coworker trust, and perceived legitimacy. The latter must retain reporting subjects, times, and material identities; all feelings cannot be inferred backward from resignation. The former also cannot consider only total pay: exit costs vary with contracts, care, opportunities, and resource-conversion conditions. [T-main；T-channels]

The temporal layer runs from immediate attention and emotion through interactional trust and handovers to organizational processes and potentially later institutional write-back. ‘Weeks’ and ‘later’ are illustrative pacing, not universal durations. A public post may change public attention without reaching the company's actual budget, appeals procedure, or household resources; meanwhile, endogenous processes such as existing contract expiry can still occur. [T-main；T-clock]

The source proposes four conditional paths: when only public relations changes while hours/appeals do not, public attention and internal trust may diverge; when resources change but meaning repair fails, staying and commitment may diverge; when care pressure is relieved, the person's option set may expand; when occupational communities provide usable bridging resources, exit costs may fall and imitation may follow. Each is a conditional path requiring checking, not a known ending, and none supplies a probability of occurrence. [T-main]

‘Resignation is due to personality’ and ‘it is entirely determined by company structure’ cannot close the question by labels. Yet the joint model does not win automatically either: compare it fairly with adequate simple explanations, checking whether added household, platform, or community circles supply independent increments. If it only draws more circles and makes the story coherent afterward, lower the gain claim. Criticism of single-line determinism cannot become universal denial that a simple mechanism may suffice for a narrow task. [T-main；T-complex]

As a bounded real-world comparison, Bray's public resignation account includes organizational position, expected material costs, and his own feelings, while distinguishing internal communication from public expression. The material supports occurrence of these expressions, not completion of household-care details or others' experiences. The artificial employee model below refers neither to him nor to his company; none of its paths can be transferred into subsequent facts of that case. [P-BRAY]

This section stops at making the joint snapshot and candidate paths visible. How transmission occurs, where branching appears, and which path is supported require the next part and event sequences and comparative materials. Who should bear costs, whether others' information may be disclosed, and what actions are authorized also cannot be inferred directly from a relationship diagram. [T-main；T-stop]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Mark the source-book example's status, fix in advance the actual case's information cutoff, and admit objects individually.

  2. 2

    Distinguish the agent, team, management, and household/community/platform, without combining them into one unified agent.

  3. 3

    Record evidence separately for membership, nesting, bridging, competition/cooperation, and temporary relationships.

  4. 4

    Tie M, Ψ, and the five clocks to materials item by item; do not read minds from actions.

  5. 5

    Write the four subsequent paths as conditional candidates and compare them with simple explanations; stop before sequence materials exist.

Distinctions to keep clear

Public resignation

An observed or publicly self-reported action.

≠

Personality explanation

Requires cross-context materials; one action cannot define a person.

Staying

The employment relationship continues.

≠

Restored commitment

A different endpoint concerning experience and investment.

Intensity of solidarity

Visible attention on a platform.

≠

Institutional repair

Procedures, rights, and actual implementation change.

Teaching construction: changed exit costs do not mean inevitable resignationTeaching scenario

AssumptionsPerson, expenses, support, and time window are entirely artificial; units are common, no costs are double-counted, and support is actually available.

Artificial employee A has a discretionary buffer of 12 units. Immediate resignation would require 10 units of living expenses until the next income and 5 units for a care transition, leaving a gap of 3. If reliable care support covers 5 units, total demand becomes 10, which the buffer covers with 2 left. The stipulations establish only removal of one financial constraint, not that A necessarily resigns or stays, or that professional meaning has been repaired.

BoundaryThis corresponds to no actual person's budget and provides no resignation advice or judgment of motives.

Teaching construction: an observation checklist for the book's four pathsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsOnly a research checklist constructed from the source, with no actual implementation or observed results.

Artificial option A changes only external messages, checking public attention and internal appeals separately; B adjusts resources and separately checks commitment; C changes care availability and checks feasible options; D has the occupational community supply actual job information, first checking receipt and usability, then exit costs and subsequent behavior. The four may combine; they are not mutually exclusive probabilistic branches.

BoundaryListing possible mechanisms does not mean they occurred; do not assign fabricated probabilities to paths.

Tim Bray's public resignation account: separating expression from causationDocumented case

No. Staying and commitment are different endpoints requiring separate evidence.

Basis: The source's second candidate path.

Is an occupational community posting job information sufficient to establish lower exit costs?

Insufficient. First check actual transmission, job availability, and relevant conversion conditions.

No. Independent channels and corresponding task comparisons are needed; where only responsibility is described, explain that use separately.

10.12Where This Part Stops ​

In briefPart Ten can now deliver a bounded joint state. Knowing who is connected to whom and how does not determine the inevitable future or grant a right to act for others.

The layer for multi-circle joint states can identify which circles need to be represented together and whether their relations are parallel, nested, overlapping, bridged, competitive, or temporary. It can also describe how memberships and roles are distributed across circles, how material and experience–meaning conditions are represented side by side, and which clocks are out of sync. It can assess whether the complex model offers a gain relative to a simple baseline.

A structural graph alone cannot establish what must happen in the future. Nor can it decide which circle most warrants protection, who should bear the costs, or who has authority to act. Event propagation, branching, and cascades belong to Part 11. Conditional foresight and bounded choice belong to Part 12. Normative judgments, authorization, and protection remain the responsibility of later layers.

If an event involves only one actor and one stable circle, and neighboring circles, membership overlap, bridging, and cross-boundary spillovers provide no additional information, do not use the full joint model. Multi-circle modeling makes it possible to preserve distinctions where interactions actually occur. An analysis need not bear that complexity every time. When fewer objects, fewer variables, and clearer evidence suffice to answer the question, the framework should scale back.

10.12Note

Understanding this section

10.12 Where this part stops

Part Ten can now deliver a bounded joint state. Knowing who is connected to whom and how does not determine the inevitable future or grant a right to act for others.

This section closes six answerable question types: which circles need simultaneous representation; how the six relationships hold along specified dimensions; how memberships and roles are distributed across circles; how M and Ψ run in parallel; which clocks are asynchronous; and whether a complex representation gains on a simple baseline for the task. ‘Can answer’ defines methodological scope, not adequate evidence in every analysis; gaps should remain as unknowns, candidates, or disputes in the snapshot. [T-main]

The future cannot be determined directly from a structural diagram: a relationship's existence only constrains possible channels; whether transmission starts, capacity suffices, delays exceed the window, and feedback returns requires additional event and dynamic materials. Part Eleven addresses event transmission, branching, and cascades; it receives a fixed state rather than automatically inferring a unique destiny from scattered labels. [T-main；T-clock]

Conditional foresight and bounded choice enter Part Twelve. Foresight adds targets, horizons, baselines, and evaluation; choice additionally compares action, delay, trials, exit, and inaction, including outcomes and implementability. Entry into the next part’s methods does not mean these evidentiary responsibilities are already met here, nor that every understanding task must escalate to prediction or intervention. [T-main]

High graph position, centrality, or propagation strength does not decide which circle deserves greater protection, who should bear costs, or who may act. These are questions of norms, authorization, and protection requiring independent grounds. Known connections may help identify whom to ask but cannot replace consent, due process, or specific authority. [T-main; T-floor]

NASA material offers a bounded comparison: the report records the Board’s mandate separately from its working relations. Researchers may describe roles and interfaces from it, but an added coordination edge creates no added authority and predicts no later measure’s effect. Only this recording boundary is used here, without evaluating every consequence of the investigation. [P-NASA]

The final simplification principle does not demand building complexity first and deleting everything afterward. If an event involves only one actor and one stable circle, with no additional information from adjacency, overlapping membership, bridging, or cross-boundary spillovers, do not activate the full joint model. Specify the task first: simplification sufficient for equipment counts may not answer member control or responsibility. Retaining necessary objects for independently grounded responsibility questions need not first prove predictive gain. [T-main; T-complex]

The strongest objection is that stopping may miss important distant relations. Preserve reopening conditions such as new independent channels, key model residuals, reversals under boundary perturbation, or upgraded use. Stopping produces a bounded answer within current material and task, not a pledge that adjacent layers will never matter; reopening also should not add imagined background indefinitely. [T-main; T-boundary]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Check whether the six question types are answered for the task, listing gaps and limits.

  2. 2

    Separate structural facts, event paths, future judgments, values/responsibility, and authorization.

  3. 3

    Enter Part Eleven for dynamic propagation; meet Part Twelve’s responsibilities for foresight/choice.

  4. 4

    Actively use a simple representation when one object/circle suffices.

  5. 5

    State reopening conditions and preserve the current version; stopping does not erase uncertainty or history.

Distinctions to keep clear

Structural channel

Specifies where an effect might travel.

≠

A determined future

Also requires triggering conditions, dynamics, timing, and comparative material.

Described subject

Records who participates in the relation.

≠

Authorized subject

Who has valid authority for a specific matter, checked separately.

Stopping

The current scope has a sufficient bounded answer.

≠

Permanent closure

Never reviewing again regardless of new information or use; this section does not support it.

Teaching construction: the same equipment, two stopping pointsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsCabinet, equipment, and count are artificial; ‘independently checked’ is stipulated, not an actual inventory conducted by the guide’s author.

An artificial warehouse inventory task asks only how many devices are inside a sealed cabinet, with an independently checked count of 8. External relations do not change counting under the setup, so a single-focus cabinet/equipment record suffices to stop. A second task asks whether 2 devices may be transferred to another organization, requiring ownership, authorization, existing uses, timing, and affected-party material. The first answer, 8, remains valid but does not answer whether transfer is allowed.

BoundaryNo transfer occurred; different uses have different evidence conditions, and description implies no action permission.

Teaching construction: an edge exists, but propagation has not startedTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAn artificial channel and stipulated nonsending, without actual organizational operations.

Artificial organizations A and B have an available safety-notice channel, but no notice was sent for this event. The joint graph may retain interface capability without recording B as having received, acted, or inevitably changed its rules next week. Later sending and receipt records would upgrade only process items; subsequent effects still need separate checks.

BoundaryA channel’s existence is neither an occurred effect nor proof that an effect is impossible.

Organizational connections and task authorization are two kinds of recordDocumented case

The Apollo 13 investigation report records both the Board’s mandate and its working links with MSC teams. Describing interfaces and tracing authority require their respective material.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If the graph connects A to B, must B already be affected?

  2. 2

    If a simple model answers a quantity question, may it answer an authority question?

  3. 3

If the graph connects A to B, must B already be affected?

Not necessarily. Check actual arrival, thresholds, capacity, and time.

Basis: The stopping boundary at the structural layer.

If a simple model answers a quantity question, may it answer an authority question?

Not directly. A changed use needs corresponding authorization and protection material.

Basis: Sufficiency varies with the task.

Must completing this part initiate actual intervention?

No. An understanding task may stop at a grounded explanation with explicit unresolved items.

Basis: This section’s layering and simplification principles.
